source.title: How Much Is a Dataset Worth? Scaling Laws, the Vendi Score, and Matrix Spectral Functions
source.authors: Jeff A. Bilmes; Gantavya Bhatt; A. Das

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses neural scaling-law forms as motivation and analyzes scaling-law-inspired data-valuation objectives, but it does not test language-model loss scaling, extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses neural scaling laws and mathematically describes an epoch-based data scaling law as piecewise power-law-like with a changing exponent and eventual saturation. That analysis does not measure language-model pretraining loss or independently test the claim versions. Its ImageNet experiments measure ResNet-18 accuracy under dataset-selection and compute-budget changes, a related but different setting; those outcomes are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper treats published scaling-law forms (Chinchilla, cluster-based, epoch-based) as set functions and proves they are submodular. It uses a power-law form to build a new appraisal function (phi1). Its experiments train ResNet-18 on ImageNet-1K subsets chosen by appraisal functions and report test accuracy. No power law is fitted in parameters, tokens or compute, and no extrapolation or allocation is tested. Its argument that scaling laws value data only by size is conceptual. The accuracy-vs-samples-seen curves are a different construct (subset quality at fixed size) and are not fitted to any law. 'discusses' would also be defensible, but no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also conclude that common scaling-law objectives and the log Vendi score are submodular, with Vendi a special case of matrix spectral functions. Directly maximizing Vendi yields subsets with worse accuracy, so it is a poor proxy at high values. Facility location is the best predictor of subset value. Size, class balance and compute budget alone do not determine data value.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies submodular data appraisal and trains ResNet-18 on selected ImageNet subsets. It does not reproduce the language-model scaling measurements or fitting procedures of the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported ImageNet outcomes vary with dataset quality and size, compute budget, class-balance constraints, and appraisal function. The paper also notes that the Gaussian-kernel width is a salient parameter in its separate coverage experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: On ImageNet ResNet-18, small class-balanced high-value subsets beat large balanced poor-value subsets at every compute budget from 0.25M to 32M samples seen. Poor subsets overfit at high compute; high-value subsets keep improving.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Held-out performance depends on data quality independently of dataset size, class balance and compute, so size-only scaling laws omit a major factor.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed subset size, runs on poor subsets with a 4M-sample budget do worse than runs on good subsets with a 1M-sample budget (Appendix K.5, Figs 15–17).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute alone is a weak predictor of test accuracy when data quality varies.

record.problems: The experiments relevant to compute and data quality use ResNet-18 on ImageNet-1K rather than language models, and report accuracy rather than pretraining loss. They do not sweep language-model parameter count, fit or compare scaling exponents, test small-run extrapolation, or optimize parameter/token allocation. Several results are presented in figures without exact tabulated values.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. The paper reports further appraisal-score correlations and coverage experiments, but these do not measure the language-model scaling quantities in the claim.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-to-large extrapolation of fitted laws.
Image-classification accuracy vs samples seen is reported, but no power-law form is fitted for image models or for repeated data.
No downstream predictability from scale or loss.
The epoch-based law is described analytically as piecewise power-law-like, but no exponents are fitted or compared.

record.verdict_notes: No rows bear on any version, so no verdicts are given. The paper's critique of scaling laws is conceptual: such laws value data only by count. It is not an empirical test of whether loss follows a power law.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power-law fits on smaller language-model runs predict much larger runs.
The compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, including how either scales with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling beyond text pretraining, including other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.
Predictability of language-model downstream-task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Empirical or comparative tests of how language-model scaling exponents and compute-optimal allocations depend on setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Trained on class-balanced ImageNet-1K subsets of different facility-location values and sizes over varied training-sample budgets.

conditions.value: high, random, and poor facility-location subsets

rows.value: The paper reports that the ranking by dataset value is largely preserved across more than two orders of magnitude of compute; high-value subsets continue improving through 32M samples seen, while poor subsets eventually overfit.
rows.uncertainty: Random subsets: 10 independent class-stratified samples at each size; figures show mean ± 1 std for random runs.
rows.locator: Section 4.1 and Figure 1; Appendix M, Figures 27–29
rows.note: This is an ImageNet ResNet-18 data-quality and compute result, not a language-model pretraining-loss scaling test.
rows.check: No fix needed. ImageNet ResNet-18 accuracy across subsets of different facility-location value; no scaling-law fit, so it bears on no version.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Compared accuracy across ImageNet-1K subset sizes while holding the training budget and configuration fixed.

conditions.value: same-size comparisons include unconstrained and class-balanced subsets

rows.value: The paper states that in every Figure 3 subplot, some runs using 5% subsets outperform runs using 20% subsets at the same compute budget.
rows.note: This indicates that subset quality affects accuracy in this image-classification setting; it does not measure language-model loss or parameter/token scaling.
rows.check: No fix needed. Fixed-compute comparison of subset size against subset value; it measures data-quality effects, not a scaling law.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
